newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PNG Prime Minister Chan sacks army chief.
newsitem.headline: PNG Prime Minister Chan sacks army chief.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan said on Tuesday he had sacked the commander of the defence force who had earlier demanded Chan resign over a decision to hire mercenaries.

Chan said in a statement the Papua New Guinea cabinet had decided late on Monday to sack Brigadier General Jerry Singirok and replace him with Colonel Alfred Aikung. Chan's statement confirmed television reports of the sackings late on Monday.
"After a meeting long into Monday night, the Papua New Guinea cabinet has removed Brigadier General Jerry Singirok from his position as Commander of the Defence Force," Chan said in the statement.

Chan said he was intensely concerned at the actions Singirok took on Monday, including demanding that Chan and his senior ministers resign within 48 hours or he would call for the government to be forced aside.

Singirok said in an "Address to the Nation" broadcast on radio on Monday that Chan's decision to employ foreign mercenaries to help end a long uprising on Bougainville island was wrong and possibly corrupt.
Much of the fighting over the past nine years has centred around the giant Panguna copper-gold mine, owned 53.6 percent by RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd.
The mine had contributed much-needed foreign capital to Papua New Guinea, which relies on exports of crude oil, gold, timber, copper and coffee for its per capita gross domestic product of US$1,228.
Australia, backed by the United States and New Zealand, has vigorously opposed Chan's plans to use mercenaries.

Singirok, promoted by Chan 15 months ago for his successful leadership on Bougainville, said he believed it was morally and ethically wrong to hire the mercenaries when the money could have been used to re-equip and boost the morale of the country's own security forces.
Eyewitnesses said the Papua New Guinea capital of Port Moresby remained calm late on Monday and troops stationed in the capital remained in their barracks.

"He may wish to state his opposition, but we have a constitution to uphold. This is nothing more than subordination and a direct threat to the constitutional democracy that Papua New Guineans hold so dear to their hearts," Chan said.
Chan said he had met with the president of the police association, Aloysius Aviaisa, who had assured him the government had the support of police.
He said he had reassured all Papua New Guinea citizens that he and the cabinet were in complete control of the situation.

Papua New Guinea, which has a population of 4.3 million mainly Melanesians, has 3,400 defence force troops and 4,600 para-military police, including riot squads used to put down frequent tribal fighting.
Australian Broadcasting Corp radio reported that Police Commissioner Bob Nenta had disassociated himself from Singirok's actions.
Earlier on Monday Singirok said he had the support of the police commissioner.
